study.title: Job 28 The wisdom that is not bought or dig
study.overview: This chapter counters two human pursuits. On the one hand, the human being demonstrates great skill to extract metals, open tunnels, divert water and discover hidden riches on earth. On the other hand, when the question is true wisdom, human effort fails: it is not found by exploitation, nor bought by gold, nor captured by observation or technique. The climax of the chapter states that wisdom consists in fearing the Lord and turning away from evil, because only God fully knows the way of wisdom and is his source.

outline.title: The human ability to explore creation
outline.explanation: The first verses describe mining, foundry, excavation and underground engineering. The man finds silver, gold, iron and copper, penetrates dark and remote places, and even changes watercourses to achieve what is precious. The point is not to exalt the technology itself, but to show the impressive range of human intelligence over nature.

outline.title: The Impossibility to Find Wisdom by Human Media
outline.explanation: After describing riches hidden on earth, the text asks where wisdom is. It is not found among the living, nor in the abyss, nor in the sea, nor can it be bought with the most valuable metals and stones. Even death and perdition only heard of it, without mastering it. The argument is that true wisdom does not belong to the market or to mere human experience.

outline.title: God knows and reveals wisdom
outline.explanation: The final answer is that God knows the way of wisdom because he sees all creation and orders his strength. He weighs the wind, measures the waters, establishes laws for rain and lightning, and then declares to the human being that wisdom is to fear the Lord and turn away from evil. Thus wisdom is at the same time a gift revealed by God and a moral path of reverence and holiness.

study.context: The chapter appears as an independent poetic speech within the book, functioning as a kind of reflective pause. The notes indicate that he summarizes the debate so far and prepares the ground for the Lord's speech. The text uses images of mining and metallurgy, activities known to the biblical author, to counterhuman dexterity in the exploitation of the earth to human limitation in the face of divine wisdom.
study.theology: Job 28 teaches that there is a decisive difference between technical knowledge and spiritual wisdom. The human being can master the processes of nature, but it does not produce for himself the correct reading of reality before God. Biblical wisdom is neither mere information, nor cunning, nor material success; it expresses itself in reverence to the Lord and in abandonment of evil. The chapter also affirms the transcendence of God: he not only knows creation, but governs it and sees its limits. At the same time, wisdom is not presented as something arbitrary or inaccessible at all, for God communicates it to the human being in the form of commandment and moral guidance. In evangelical reading, this points to the need for dependence on God, intellectual humility and obedient life.

scholarViews.insight: The chapter is an autonomous speech that, according to the note, can function as the author's poetic interlude to summarize the failure of human wisdom and prepare the Lord's speeches.

The description of the riches of the earth shows how much human beings strive for material goods, but this does not prove that they understand the ways of providence; digging the earth is not the same as to probe the counsels of heaven.
The question about the origin of wisdom is resumed until it concludes that God is his source and that the human being finds it when he lives in the fear of the Lord and departs from evil.

questions: If humanity manages to exploit the earth with such competence, why do they fail to seek wisdom to live before God?
In what ways can I be valuing more what is precious to the market than what is precious to the Lord?
What, in practice, does it mean to fear the Lord and turn away from evil in my concrete decisions this week?
study.practice: Take a break a time to examine your priorities in the light of this chapter: what goals, goods or abilities have occupied the place of wisdom? Pray asking God for discernment to choose what is right, to reject evil in a concrete way and to submit his intelligence, work and ambitions to the fear of the Lord. Practice a specific step of obedience today, not just an abstract reflection.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided treat the chapter as a poetic unit and suggest, without stating as an indisputable fact, that it is perhaps the voice of the narrator or an interlude of the author. There are also limitations in the notes of Matthew Henry, which appear truncated; therefore, the synthesis depends only on the excerpts presented. It is not possible to safely determine, from the notes, all the historical or literary intentions of the biblical author.
